landmarks.name: Victoria Falls
landmarks.writeup: One of the largest and most famous waterfalls in the world, located on the Zambezi River at the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia.

wiki.extract: Victoria Falls, popularly known as Vic Falls, is a resort town and city in the province of Matabeleland North, Zimbabwe. It lies on the southern bank of the Zambezi River at the western end of Victoria Falls themselves. According to the 2022 Population Census, the town had a population of 35,199.

landmarks.name: Great Zimbabwe Ruins
landmarks.writeup: Ancient city ruins that were the capital of the Kingdom of Zimbabwe during the Late Iron Age, showcasing impressive stone architecture.

wiki.extract: Great Zimbabwe was a city in the south-eastern hills of the modern country of Zimbabwe, near Masvingo. It was settled from around 1000 CE, and served as the capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe from the 13th century. It is the largest stone structure in precolonial Southern Africa. Major construction on the city began in the 11th century until the 15th century, and it was abandoned in the 16th or 17th century. The edifices were erected by ancestors of the Shona people, currently located in Zimbabwe and nearby countries. The stone city spans an area of 7.22 square kilometres (2.79 mi2). Population estimates vary. Earlier estimates suggest a peak population of around 20,000 people. A recent study using archaeological, ethnographic, and historical evidence, along with statistical modeling suggests that the site's population did not exceed 10,000 people. The Zimbabwe state centred on it likely covered 50,000 km². It is recognised as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO.

landmarks.name: Hwange National Park
landmarks.writeup: Zimbabwe's largest game reserve, home to a wide variety of wildlife including elephants, lions, and buffalo.

wiki.extract: Hwange National Park is the largest natural reserve in Zimbabwe. It measures around 14,600 km2 (5,600 sq mi) in area. It lies in the northwest of the country, just off the main road between Bulawayo and Victoria Falls. The nearest town is Dete.

cultural_events.name: Harare International Festival of the Arts (HIFA)
cultural_events.writeup: An annual arts festival showcasing music, theater, dance, and visual arts from Zimbabwe and around the world.

wiki.extract: The Harare International Festival of the Arts (HIFA) is one of Africa's largest international arts festivals. Established in 1999 by Manuel Bagorro the festival takes place each year in late April or early May in Harare, the capital of Zimbabwe. The week-long festival encompasses five principal disciplines: theatre, music, dance, fine art, and poetry.

cultural_events.name: Zimbabwe International Film Festival
cultural_events.writeup: A platform for local and international filmmakers to present their work and promote Zimbabwean cinema.

wiki.extract: Zimbabwe International Film Festival  is an annual ten-day film festival held in Zimbabwe in August or September. Instituted in 1998, it is organised by the Zimbabwe International Film Festival Trust (ZIFFT), a non-profit organisation. The festival is a non-political competitive platform that provides a showcase of feature films, documentary films and short films, as well as providing workshops and other cultural events.

food_writeup: Zimbabwean cuisine features staple foods like sadza (a maize meal porridge), often served with meat, vegetables, and relishes. Traditional dishes include nyama (grilled meat) and mopane worms.
brief_history: Zimbabwe was formerly known as Rhodesia under British colonial rule. It gained independence in 1980 after a protracted liberation struggle. The country has experienced political and economic challenges since independence.

important_people.name: Robert Mugabe
important_people.description: Former Prime Minister and President, key figure in Zimbabwe's independence.

current_conflicts: Zimbabwe faces ongoing economic challenges, political tensions, and issues related to land reform and governance, but no active armed conflicts.

commentary.inflation_management: Zimbabwe's inflation record is among the world's worst. After the 2008 hyperinflation ended with dollarization in 2009, inflation was contained at 0-4% through 2018 (even -2.4% in 2015). The 2019 return of the Zimbabwe dollar restarted the cycle: 255.3% in 2019, 557.2% in 2020, 98.5% in 2021, 193.4% in 2022, 667.4% in 2023, and a series high of 736.1% in 2024. On April 5, 2024, the Reserve Bank launched the ZiG, a gold-backed currency replacing the Zimdollar; inflation fell to a projected 81.4% in 2025, still catastrophic. The central bank has no credibility left after four currency regimes in fifteen years; dollarization of transactions (about 85%) is the population's verdict.
commentary.debt_management: Zimbabwe's debt is modest by the standards of its monetary chaos, because hyperinflation repeatedly wiped out domestic obligations and external arrears are simply not serviced. From 26.4% of GDP in 2013, the series low, the ratio rose as the government borrowed domestically and accumulated arrears: 76.1% in 2023, the series high, easing to a projected 43.8% in 2025 largely through exchange-rate effects. Zimbabwe is in arrears to the World Bank, AfDB, and bilateral creditors, and cannot borrow externally until they are cleared; the 2022-24 structured dialogue on arrears clearance made limited progress. The debt numbers understate the true burden, which includes massive contingent liabilities and unrecorded obligations.

key_events.event: Hyperinflation peaked; dollarization (2009) ended the crisis; inflation fell to single digits.
Mugabe ousted in a military transition (November 2017); Mnangagwa took power.
Zimbabwe dollar reintroduced; inflation surged past 500% by 2020.
Disputed 2023 elections kept Mnangagwa in power; inflation hit 667.4%.
April 5, 2024: gold-backed ZiG currency launched to replace the collapsed Zimdollar.
Inflation projected at 81.4% in 2025 as the ZiG struggled to gain acceptance.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued monetary instability: the ZiG's survival depends on fiscal discipline the government has never shown, and 81% inflation in 2025 suggests the cycle is repeating. Upside would require genuine reform, arrears clearance, and re-engagement with creditors; downside is another full hyperinflation. Uncertainty is high on policy but the direction is familiar: Zimbabwe has run this experiment four times, and the population's dollarization is the rational response.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections. Note: the IMF inflation series for Zimbabwe begins in 2009 (hyperinflation years excluded).
